clue.text: One endemic disorder amusing performer? Not him!

indicators.note: disorder tells us the letters of the two words before it are thrown into a jumble

explanation.surface: A medical-sounding remark about a widespread disorder, oddly linked to an entertainer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disorder' looks like part of a medical phrase but is the anagram signal for ONE ENDEMIC. 'Not him!' narrows the funny performer to a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A female comic is an entertainer who amuses, and 'Not him!' rules out the male form.

clue.text: Systematically search English valley

parts.note: to comb an area is to search it thoroughly

explanation.surface: A search through an English valley.
explanation.definitionFit: A combe is a short steep hollow in a hillside, chiefly in southern England.

clue.text: Fights Robert, holding many a dangerous weapon

parts.note: mills is old slang for fist fights

indicators.note: holding means the shortened name has the letter for many inside it

parts.note: Bob is a short form of Robert
M, the Roman numeral for a thousand, stands for many

explanation.surface: Robert in a series of fights, armed with plenty of dangerous weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: A Mills bomb is the classic British hand grenade of the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: This hand grenade was a lethal piece of military armament.

clue.text: Result of lack of will in female I spotted far off?

indicators.note: spotted in the sense of dotted or placed, so the letters are set down within the phrase for far off

parts.note: in the distance means far off
taken as written
her is a female pronoun

explanation.surface: A woman spotting something a long way off, oddly linked to an absent will.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spotted' looks like 'seen', but here means set down or placed, so the pieces go inside the phrase for far off. The '?' flags the loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being cut off from an inheritance is the outcome when a will leaves an heir nothing.

clue.text: City I found, in total, a delightful place

parts.note: Ely is a small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

indicators.note: in tells us the letter I goes inside the word for total

parts.note: a sum is a total

explanation.surface: Someone finds a pleasant city, all told.
explanation.walkthrough: ELY is an English cathedral city in Cambridgeshire. 'found' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Elysium was the Greek paradise of the blessed dead, hence any state of bliss.

clue.text: Simpletons often in the soup

explanation.surface: Fools who are frequently in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the soup' suggests being in trouble, but literally pasta strands float in soup.
explanation.definitionFit: Noodle is slang for a fool; and strips of pasta are commonly served in broth.

clue.text: A lawgiver — e's not there to be a prophet

indicators.note: not there tells us the named letters are missing from the lawgiver's name

parts.note: Moses brought the Ten Commandments, the biblical lawgiver
e's read as the letters E and S

explanation.surface: A biblical lawgiver missing a letter becomes a different prophet.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints e's, which the OCR misread; 'not there' signals the removal of those two letters from the biblical lawgiver.
explanation.definitionFit: Amos is a minor prophet of the Old Testament with a book under his name.

clue.text: Satisfied about part of Bible and music for service

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word for satisfied surrounds the part of the Bible

parts.note: to meet a need is to satisfy it, so met means satisfied
OT is the Old Testament, one part of the Bible

explanation.surface: A churchgoer content with Bible readings and church music.
explanation.definitionFit: A motet is a short sacred choral composition sung in church.

clue.text: A fraction beyond the 1st XV?

explanation.surface: A small part, or a player not quite good enough for the top rugby team.
explanation.walkthrough: A rugby union side has fifteen players (XV), so the next one along, just outside the first team, would be number sixteen.
explanation.definitionFit: One part of a whole divided by sixteen; and the position just after the fifteen players of a first team.

clue.text: Old king unlikely to get drunk quickly

explanation.surface: An ancient monarch who could hold his drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a giant wine bottle holding about twenty standard bottles, hard to finish quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Babylonian ruler who took Jerusalem; and an enormous wine bottle of about fifteen litres.

clue.text: Wine spoiling my meals, though it did for Clarence

indicators.note: spoiling suggests the words my meals are ruined and their letters reworked

explanation.surface: A wine that ruins dinner, though it proved fatal for a duke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'though it did for Clarence' is a historical aside: the Duke of Clarence was said to have been drowned in a butt of this wine in 1478.
explanation.definitionFit: Malmsey is a sweet fortified Madeira, a kind of strong dessert drink.

clue.text: Demand too much from public before a vote

parts.note: overt means open or public, not hidden
X is the mark made on a ballot paper when voting

explanation.surface: A complaint that a government asks too much of people just before an election.
explanation.definitionFit: To overburden someone with excessive claims or effort is to overstrain them in this sense.

clue.text: Must get right away from German city trial

parts.note: Essen is an industrial city in the Ruhr

indicators.note: away tells us the letter for right is removed from trial

explanation.surface: An instruction to leave a trial in a German city at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Must get right away' reads as urgency, but 'Must' is the noun (a must) and 'right away' means drop R from TRIAL, leaving TIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A must is something indispensable, a necessity that cannot be done without.

clue.text: 'ound that is loose

parts.note: 'ound is hound with its h dropped, so read hound as the verb hunt and drop its h too
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A Cockney remark that a dog has got free.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe signals an aitch-dropping accent: hound (pursue) is HUNT, said without its H as 'UNT.
explanation.definitionFit: To loose something is to unfasten or release it, a verb sense of setting free.

clue.text: River horse, so to speak

indicators.note: so to speak tells us the word for horse is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a roan is a horse with a coat of mixed white and coloured hairs

explanation.surface: A horse described as being a river, figuratively.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhône is a major waterway flowing from Switzerland through France to the Mediterranean.

clue.text: He fixes things for two sorts of traveller

parts.note: a rep, a sales representative, is a commercial traveller
an airman travels by air as a flyer

explanation.surface: A mechanic who serves two kinds of travelling people.
explanation.definitionFit: A mechanic or handyman mends broken items for a living.

clue.text: Grotesque emphasis wrongly attached to name

indicators.note: wrongly tells us the letters of emphasis are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A complaint that someone's name has been stressed in a bizarre way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'attached to' is a link joining the anagram of EMPHASIS to N.
explanation.definitionFit: Something deformed or distorted in shape looks grotesque.

clue.text: Old man wandering again to part of South America

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father, an old man

indicators.note: wandering tells us the letters of again to roam into a new order

explanation.surface: An old man roaming once more towards South America.
explanation.definitionFit: Patagonia is the southern region of Argentina and Chile.

clue.text: Brings out books from the bar, having left one novels

parts.note: a pub is a bar where drinks are served
I is the Roman numeral for one
She is the H. Rider Haggard novel, so several copies of it are Shes

explanation.surface: Someone takes books out of a pub, having abandoned a single novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novels' is plural because SHE, Rider Haggard's novel, is taken as countable: several copies make SHES.
explanation.definitionFit: A publisher issues books to the public, putting new titles on sale.

clue.text: In Asian port, rather frequent visitor

indicators.note: in tells us the word for rather goes inside the name of the port

parts.note: Hue is a city and river port in central Vietnam
a bit means rather, somewhat

explanation.surface: A regular visitor at a port in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rather frequent' looks like one phrase, but 'rather' gives A BIT and 'frequent visitor' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A habitué is a regular at a place such as a café or club.

clue.text: Colourful ballad singer's home town

explanation.surface: A vivid description of where a folk singer was born.
explanation.walkthrough: In the ballad Barbara Allen the singer begins 'In Scarlet Town, where I was born'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bright red shade; and the town named in the old ballad Barbara Allen.

clue.text: Throw overboard in the Channel!

explanation.surface: An order to dump something into the sea between England and France.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ditch is old slang for the English Channel; 'in' simply joins the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: To jettison or discard is one sense; the other is the slang nickname for the narrow sea separating England from France.

clue.text: Units evacuated from Indonesia land in Asia

indicators.note: evacuated from tells us the units are cleared out of the word Indonesia

parts.note: ones are units, single things

explanation.surface: Military units pulled out of Indonesia, a country in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing ONES from INDONESIA leaves the letters I, N, D, I, A.
explanation.definitionFit: India is a large country on the Asian subcontinent.

clue.text: Sounds like Alice's pet customer in restaurant

indicators.note: sounds like tells us the pet's name is heard, not spelt

parts.note: Dinah is Alice's cat in Alice in Wonderland

explanation.surface: Someone eating in a restaurant who resembles a little girl's pet.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech, without a sounded final r, DINAH and DINER sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A diner is someone eating a meal, a patron of an eating place.

clue.text: So began broadcast, without hesitation, from loudspeaker

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the rearranged letters surround the hesitation
broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters of so began are spread about

parts.note: er is the sound of a hesitation

explanation.surface: A speech that began on air without any stumbling, delivered through a speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' but means outside: the anagram of SO BEGAN wraps round ER. 'loudspeaker' is a person, not a device.
explanation.definitionFit: Boanerges, 'sons of thunder' in the Gospels, came to mean any loud, ranting preacher or orator.

clue.text: Board intended to support position of discarded worker

explanation.surface: A plank put up to hold things, or where a sacked employee ends up.
explanation.walkthrough: A worker 'on the shelf' has been laid aside as no longer wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A ledge for holding items; and, in the idiom on the shelf, the place of someone put aside.

clue.text: Island breed used to flog offenders there?

explanation.surface: A tailless cat that, on its home island, doubles as a whip for punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man kept judicial birching long after mainland Britain; the 'cat' (cat-o'-nine-tails) was a whip, so a Manx cat is also that island's whip.
explanation.definitionFit: The tailless feline breed from the Isle of Man; and, punningly, a whip such as the cat-o'-nine-tails used on that island.

clue.text: Medical treatment — might have one up in arms

definitions.text: might have one up in arms

explanation.surface: A remedy that could put someone on the warpath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up in arms' suggests anger, but means displayed on a coat of arms: the lozenge is a diamond shape in heraldry.
explanation.definitionFit: A medicated tablet sucked for a sore throat; and a diamond-shaped charge in heraldry.

clue.text: Artless female?

parts.note: artless read as having no Royal Academician, no artist: NO plus RA
RA stands for a Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: A naive woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artless' seems to describe a naive woman, but is read literally as lacking an artist, the Royal Academician.
explanation.definitionFit: Nora is a woman's given name, so it stands for an example of a female person.

clue.text: Spouse improved a fraction

parts.note: better means improved, made more fit
a half is a fraction

explanation.surface: A wife or husband who got slightly better.
explanation.definitionFit: One's better half is an affectionate idiom for one's husband or wife.
